Cash discount or zero-interest financing: compare equal resources and the same final date

Track the upfront price, cash retained, instalment debt and account balances when an immediate-payment discount competes with a hypothetical interest-free payment plan.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare the same purchase, starting cash and monthly budget

Interactive planning lab

Cash purchase price now$9,500
Equal monthly financing payment$416.67
Financing advantage at the common end date-$316.36

One invented all-in purchase, no financed interest and no down payment. Cash discount applies only to immediate full payment; a separate financing fee is paid upfront. Both choices start with purchase price plus the financing fee in cash and receive the same monthly amount, equal to one instalment. The cash buyer saves that monthly amount; the financed buyer uses it for the payment. Accounts earn the same constant entered return after tax and costs before each month-end flow. Both finish with the same item and no purchase debt. No actual credit terms, statutory APR, late charges, default, resale value or return guarantee is calculated.

On this page

  1. Record both all-in prices before comparing the payment size
  2. Separate zero interest from zero additional cost
  3. Give both choices the same starting cash and monthly resources
  4. Read the cash balance and the debt together
  5. Test the account return without treating it as an available offer
  6. Bring the comparison back to the actual cash commitment

The central idea

A zero interest rate does not remove a forgone cash discount or an upfront fee. Compare the same starting resources and monthly budget, then subtract debt before interpreting retained cash.

01

Record both all-in prices before comparing the payment size

A merchant may offer a discount for immediate full payment alongside an instalment plan advertised with no interest. The choice includes the purchase price and the calendar of payments. A small instalment alone does not describe the total amount committed.

The default purchase has an all-in price of CAD 10,000. Paying in full now receives a hypothetical 5% discount, producing a CAD 9,500 cash price. The alternative finances the full CAD 10,000 over twenty-four equal month-end payments and charges a separate CAD 100 upfront fee. The item is identical in both cases.

Quebec’s Office de la protection du consommateur discusses financing promotions, including possible immediate-payment discounts and charges when promotional conditions are not met. This example does not apply a province’s legal rules. Its simplified contract always receives every payment on time and charges no interest on the instalment principal.

02

Separate zero interest from zero additional cost

Dividing CAD 10,000 by twenty-four gives an unrounded monthly payment of CAD 416.666…. The calculator keeps fractional cents internally so the principal is fully repaid at the selected final date. An actual lender may round payments and adjust the last instalment.

The nominal total paid under financing is CAD 10,100: CAD 10,000 of principal plus the CAD 100 upfront fee. The immediate-payment price is CAD 9,500. The CAD 600 difference consists of the CAD 500 forgone discount and the CAD 100 fee.

That CAD 600 is a comparison of purchase payments before any return on money retained. It is not a statutory annual percentage rate, an annualized borrowing charge or an investment loss. Describing the financed principal as interest-free can coexist with a higher total purchase payment when the alternative price is discounted.

03

Give both choices the same starting cash and monthly resources

A comparison can accidentally favour financing if it invests the cash retained but ignores the payments coming from future income. The model therefore gives both choices identical resources: opening cash equal to the undiscounted price plus the financing fee, and an available monthly amount equal to one instalment.

Under the defaults, both start with CAD 10,100. The cash buyer pays CAD 9,500, leaving CAD 600 in the account. The financed buyer pays the CAD 100 fee, leaving CAD 10,000 in the account and owing CAD 10,000 on the purchase.

At each month-end, the financed buyer uses the available CAD 416.666… to make the payment. The cash buyer saves the same amount. Both accounts receive the same assumed return before that month-end flow. Neither path receives an extra contribution that is unavailable to the other, and no instalment is silently paid from an unmodeled source.

04

Read the cash balance and the debt together

The account-balance chart shows how much money is retained or saved. At the beginning, financing appears to retain much more cash: CAD 10,000 compared with CAD 600. It also carries the purchase debt. That liability needs to remain visible when comparing financial positions.

The next chart subtracts remaining purchase debt from the financed account. At index zero, that net position is zero, while the cash buyer has CAD 600 and no purchase debt. The identical item is excluded from both sides, so its value is not counted twice or assigned a different resale price to favour one choice.

Purchase debt declines by an equal amount after each instalment and reaches zero after month twenty-four. At that common endpoint, the account comparison and the account-minus-debt comparison coincide. An earlier cash balance is a liquidity observation; the final net position answers a different question about the resources remaining after this purchase debt has been repaid.

05

Test the account return without treating it as an available offer

The default account return is a hypothetical 3% effective annual rate after taxes and costs. It is converted to a monthly compound rate using (1 + annual rate)1/12 − 1. The calculator does not simply divide the effective annual rate by twelve.

At a zero account return, the cash buyer finishes with CAD 10,600: its initial CAD 600 plus CAD 10,000 of later savings. The financed buyer finishes with CAD 10,000. Financing’s endpoint advantage is therefore negative CAD 600, matching the nominal purchase-payment difference. This is a useful reconciliation of the two ledgers.

At the default 3% annual return, the financed account ends at CAD 10,609 and the cash buyer’s account at about CAD 10,925.36. Financing’s endpoint advantage is therefore negative CAD 316.36. A positive return gives the financed buyer more time earning on retained cash, while the cash buyer earns on a smaller opening balance and later deposits. The matrix compares that timing effect with different cash discounts. Higher-return rows are conditional arithmetic, not forecasts, deposit quotations or evidence that an uncertain investment can safely fund a fixed payment commitment.

06

Bring the comparison back to the actual cash commitment

Confirm the total payable, discount eligibility, any deposit, mandatory fee, tax timing and each due date. A plan requiring an immediate tax payment or a final balloon payment is different from the equal month-end principal schedule shown here. Replace the schedule rather than hiding a different payment pattern inside the return input.

The model assumes the monthly resource is available throughout the term. It does not test job loss, a missed payment, a promotional-rate expiry, accelerated collection or charges arising from a broken condition. A real payment plan needs enough accessible cash to meet its actual dates, even if an endpoint comparison looks favourable.

Use both the total-payment chart and the account-minus-debt chart. The first identifies the immediate discount and fee trade-off; the second applies equal resources over time. The result is a transparent comparison of an invented contract, rather than a recommendation to borrow, invest the proceeds or choose a particular financing provider.
